title: Biomechanical Phenotyping Pipeline for Stalk Lodging Resistance in Maize
author: Tabaracci, Bokros, et al.

steps.title: Remove stalks from field
steps.instruction: After completing DARLING testing, cut each stalk at ground level with garden shears or loppers, remove any remaining leaves, and verify that the barcode tag remains firmly attached.

steps.title: Rejoin broken stalks
steps.instruction: If a stalk has broken into two pieces, fasten the halves together using Velcro.

steps.title: Bag stalks by plot
steps.instruction: Place all stalks from a single plot into one burlap bag, then label the bag with the row tag that includes the plot number in both numeric and barcode format.

steps.title: Dry stalks in greenhouse
steps.instruction: Spread the labeled burlap bags evenly throughout a greenhouse set to 100 °F with fans running continuously; dry the stalks for six weeks, avoiding any stacking of bags and rotating each bag twice a week to promote uniform drying.

steps.title: Adjust drying conditions if needed
steps.instruction: If local relative humidity, ambient temperature, or initial stalk moisture differ, modify the greenhouse temperature and/or drying duration accordingly; alternatively, for a small number of samples, use a forced‑air dryer.

steps.title: Store dried stalks
steps.instruction: After drying, keep the stalks at room temperature in a climate‑controlled laboratory or storage area; they remain stable for several years without noticeable degradation of material properties.

steps.title: Clean stalks before lab testing
steps.instruction: Snip any remaining brace‑root segments as close to the node as possible, peel off any residual leaf sheaths, and firmly re‑secure any barcode tags that have become loose.

steps.title: Record stalk identity
steps.instruction: Scan each stalk’s QR code using the portable Bluetooth‑enabled barcode scanner employed in the field to log its identity for all subsequent laboratory data collection.

description: Phenotypes at numerous spatial scales contribute to stalk lodging. Methods for measuring phenotypes at the plant level (plant height, ear height, structural bending stiffness, and structural bending strength), organ level (major and minor diameter, rind thickness, internode length, linear density, rind penetration resistance and integrated puncture score) and tissue level (chemical composition, tissue bending strength and Young's modulus) are presented. The methodologies are presented below in the chronological order in which they are typically acquired.
